# Diagnosing the Steed 5: Turbo Leaks and Injector Failures

Your 2016 Steed 5 2.0L exhibiting over-revving behavior alongside a non-start condition immediately after power removal points to a specific set of mechanical failures interacting with the engine's fuel and boost management systems. The symptoms you describedâspecifically the engine continuing to run without ignition or battery power, and the requirement to be in gear to stopâare classic indicators of an uncontrolled combustion event rather than a standard stalling issue.

The turbocharger leak you identified is likely the primary driver of the over-revving condition. In a direct-injection setup like the 2.0L found in this vehicle, the turbo acts as a variable geometry or fixed-geometry compressor that forces air into the intake manifold. If the seal between the compressor and turbine housing fails, or if there is an internal bypass valve sticking open, unmetered air enters the cylinders. Modern Engine Control Units (ECUs) attempt to compensate for this by retarding ignition timing or reducing fuel delivery to prevent detonation. However, if the boost pressure exceeds the ECU's ability to modulate the throttle plate and injectors, the engine will surge up the rev range. The ECU effectively "loses" its ability to limit RPM because it cannot create a vacuum seal against the high-pressure air leaking from the turbo shaft or housing.

The fact that you had to put the vehicle in gear for the engine to stop suggests a failure of the idle control system combined with a lack of load. When the transmission is in neutral, the throttle plate remains open slightly to maintain idle speed. If the ECU detects a massive boost leak or a missing injector signal (due to the two non-functional injectors), it may enter a limp mode where it opens the throttle fully to maintain airflow while trying to stabilize RPM. Shifting into gear loads the crankshaft mechanically; once the transmission engages, the resistance provided by the drivetrain prevents the engine from spinning freely, effectively acting as a physical governor that overrides the ECU's inability to control the idle speed under high-vacuum/high-boost conditions.

The observation that the engine runs after removing the key and battery confirms that there is still enough compression and residual fuel in the cylinders to sustain combustion once ignited. The lack of spark or fuel cut-off from the ECU (due to total power loss) means the fire continues until it burns out all available oxygen or fuel. This behavior also explains why the engine failed to restart upon reconnecting power; the ECU may have entered a protective state preventing fuel injection while the system self-checks, or the cylinder compression is so low due to the turbo leak that starting is impossible.

The two non-working injectors exacerbate this scenario by creating a severe air-fuel imbalance. If the engine runs on one side of the bank with missing cylinders, it creates uneven combustion pressures that can cause the crankshaft to rotate erratically. This irregular firing order confuses the ECU's timing calculations, making it harder for the system to manage boost pressure effectively.

### Recommended Diagnostic Path

Before attempting further diagnostics or repairs, address the mechanical integrity of the turbocharger immediately. A leaking turbo is a source of uncontrolled pressure that can damage valves and gaskets throughout the intake tract. Verify the leak by inspecting the compressor side of the turbo for oil residue or air hissing sounds when the engine is off.

Regarding the injectors, you must determine if this is an electrical failure (circuit open/short) or a mechanical clog. Use a multimeter to check resistance across the injector coils and verify the power supply at the connector while the ignition is on. If the ECU reports a "fuel pump pressure low" or "injector circuit malfunction" code, these codes should align with the two injectors you identified as non-functional.

Repairing the turbo may require replacing the entire unit or rebuilding the shaft and seals if available. Restoring injector functionality will likely involve replacing the faulty coils or the entire injector assembly. Once these components are restored, clear any stored fault codes using an OBD-II scanner to allow the ECU to relearn idle characteristics without the previous mechanical faults interfering with its logic.
